title: Holy time, not holy place
hookLine: Shabbat is built in time; it begins at sundown on Friday and ends at nightfall Saturday

lines: A HOLY PLACE THAT COMES TO YOU.
cards: People cross oceans to stand somewhere holy. A cathedral. A mountaintop.
A shrine at the end of a long road. Jewish tradition also keeps a holy place you don't travel to at all, because it travels to you.

It arrives every week, on the same day, wherever you are: a hospital room, a dorm, a kitchen in a small apartment. You can't buy a ticket to it, and you can't be too far away from it. It just comes, at sundown, on Friday.

teach.h: THE FIRST HOLY THING WAS A DAY.
teach.b: Go back to the first chapters of Genesis. God makes light, sky, sea, land, stars, animals and people, and calls them good. But the first thing the Torah calls holy isn't any of them.
It's a day. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Hallowed means made holy, kadosh in Hebrew.
Before there was a holy mountain or a holy tent, there was a holy time. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel built a whole book on that observation.

He described Shabbat as a sanctuary built in time instead of in space, a palace people enter once a week and leave at the end of the day. Yesterday's mishkan was a tent you could carry. Shabbat is even more portable.
The Jewish day starts in the evening, because Genesis says there was evening and there was morning.
So Shabbat begins at sundown on Friday. Candles are lit a little before sunset, and it ends on Saturday night when three stars can be seen in the sky. A little more than a full day.
In that time, observant Jews stop the kind of work that makes and changes the world, and spend the day on rest, meals, prayer, family, study and friends.
Others keep parts of it: a Friday dinner, candles, an unplugged afternoon.
Jewish movements differ on how Shabbat is kept, and Jews find their own places on that range.

teach.h: AND GOD BLESSED THE SEVENTH DAY.
teach.b: What they share is the idea underneath: some things can't be made in space. They can only be kept in time.

how: Shabbat begins at sundown on Friday and ends when three stars appear on Saturday night; many Jewish families mark it with candles, a festive meal and a day set apart from work.

o: Shabbat: a day made holy, not a place
a holy season like the week of Passover
the set hours for daily prayer at synagogue

games.q: what's inside holy time — tap the pairs.

s: the first thing the Torah calls holy is a place
it's a day: God blessed the seventh day and hallowed it.
the Jewish day begins in the evening
there was evening and there was morning, so Shabbat starts at sundown Friday.
all Jews keep Shabbat in exactly the same way
Jewish movements and families keep it in different ways; the idea of holy time is shared.

games.q: you're reading Genesis for the first time. God has made light, land, stars and people. what's the first thing called holy?
games.why: "and God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it": the first holy thing is a stretch of time.

practice: Look at the week ahead like a calendar on the wall, and find one hour, Friday night, Saturday afternoon, or any hour that works for your life, to spend without producing, fixing, buying or posting anything.
Picture it: where you'd be, who'd be there, what you'd do instead. Then mark it, in your head or in your phone.

wordCard.voice: Holy time. Shabbat, the first thing the Torah calls holy: a day, not a place, from sundown Friday to nightfall Saturday.

orig.note: Hebrew: holy, set apart. Kiddush and kedushah come from the same root.

carryVoice: Your line: a palace in time. You don't travel to it; it comes to you. Day ninety-seven, done.
